items.title: The gun within: Crimes involving police officers rise to 248
items.description: Report reveals an increase in cases of officers pointing guns at their colleagues and themselves.
content: Crime incidents also include suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
Police constable Raphael Ojiambo, 24, was shot dead at the Wikithuki Border Patrol Unit training camp in Tseikuru, Kitui County on October 25, 2024.
Investigations pointed to the young officer being killed by another constable, Hussein Yusuf Ali, who was arrested three kilometres from the camp a day later.
The two officers had recently graduated from the Administration Police Training College in Embakasi and were undergoing further training before deployment to the Border Patrol Unit.

In Eldoret, Uasin Gishu County, police constable Lillian Biwott was arrested on September 5, 2026, after allegedly shooting and killing her husband, Victor Kipchumba, following a long-running family dispute.
Biwott, an Administration Police officer attached to the Kenya Bureau of Standards, reportedly returned home after reporting for duty before the argument escalated into the shooting.
Crime incidents also include suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
Uasin Gishu County Police Commander Benjamin Mwanthi confirmed that the suspect was being held and would be arraigned in court.
The two are among more than 250 crime incidents involving police officers in the past year.
A report on national security tabled before Parliament by President William Ruto has revealed that crimes involving police officers increased to 248 between September, 2025 and August, 2026.
Since conclusion of the report, there have been more incidents, for instance the murder of Raphael Ojiambo.

The National Police Service has advertised for recruitment of officers, less than a year after a similar exercise that netted 10,000 new recruits. A source at the NPS said that the fresh exercise is targeting 5,000 recruits.

As part of initiatives to lower the number of crimes involving police officers, the National Police Service Commission has established a counselling unit to support officers facing mental-health and substance-abuse challenges. Police authorities have also acknowledged the trauma associated with maintaining law and order in difficult circumstances.

On January 14, 2026, a Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) ranger, John Ndichu, allegedly shot dead Police Constable Stanley Karithi in Kinango, Kwale County, following a disagreement over two goats reportedly collected for Christmas festivities.
The ranger also shot and wounded another police officer and a boda boda rider before turning his weapon on himself.

In some cases, the violence has unfolded inside police stations and officers’ quarters. In others, it has spilled into homes, workplaces and public spaces, leaving families devastated and raising concerns about the safeguards governing the use of government-issued weapons.

According to police accounts, the disagreement arose after officers questioned Ndichu about two goats allegedly donated by a rancher for Christmas celebrations but which had not been handed over as expected.
The ranger reportedly became angry, picked up his AK-47 rifle and opened fire.
The incident illustrated how seemingly minor disputes between personnel serving in uniformed agencies can escalate into deadly confrontations when firearms are readily accessible.
Away from the workplace, a series of incidents involving serving officers has also raised concerns about domestic violence and the use of service weapons in family disputes.

On July 20, 2026, Administration Police Sergeant John Kamau Ikenye allegedly shot dead his partner, Betha Wanja Gachoki, before turning his G3 rifle on himself at their staff quarters at Karoti Girls High School in Mwea East, Kirinyaga County.
The bodies were discovered after colleagues became concerned when Ikenye failed to report for duty.
Preliminary investigations indicated that Wanja had sustained gunshot wounds while lying in bed, while the officer was found seated in the sitting room with the rifle.
A neighbour, who said the couple had lived together for about three years, expressed disbelief at the tragedy.

“I used to buy items from his wife’s shop. They were very friendly. The lady comes from Difathas and they had been together for three years. We wonder what went wrong,” said Kimbimbi resident Stella Wangui.
Read: Kenyan embassy warns non-Muslims against entering Mecca holy sites
Another neighbour said residents had heard gunshots but did not immediately appreciate their significance.

“We heard gunshots at around 4am but did not take them seriously. Later, we were shocked to learn that a police officer had killed his wife and then committed suicide. We suspect they may have quarrelled, although we do not know the cause,” the neighbour said.

The incident followed another shooting in Naivasha on January 1, 2026, when Corporal Collins Kochei allegedly shot Lucy Wanjiru Njoroge, a 34-year-old bar owner, before turning his AK-47 rifle on himself.
Kochei, who was attached to Tangi Tano Police Post in Gilgil, died after being rushed to hospital, while Njoroge was admitted in critical condition.
Detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations launched investigations into the shooting.
The incidents have also included suspected suicides in which officers used their service firearms.
On February 17, 2026, Constable Joseph Komolomoi was found dead in his house at Forolle Police Lines in Marsabit County after allegedly shooting himself with his AK-47 rifle.
Colleagues reportedly heard a gunshot before breaking into the locked house and finding his body.
A note was recovered from the house, although police said it would undergo forensic examination to establish its authenticity.
On May 14, 2026, a police constable attached to Daystar Police Post in Athi River reportedly shot himself at his residence following a domestic disagreement with his 23-year-old spouse.
He was rushed to hospital in Mlolongo before being transferred to another facility in Kikuyu, where he later died.
A police report indicated that the firearm used had been officially issued to him. Investigators recovered a Scorpion rifle and a spent 9mm cartridge from the scene.
On June 2, 2026, another officer attached to the Diplomatic Police Unit and assigned to a Member of Parliament was found dead in his rented house in Kasarani, Nairobi.
Police recovered his service firearm and treated the incident as a suspected suicide pending investigations.

In Laikipia, Constable Peter Macharia Mwangi shot and killed 29-year-old Benson Kipkemboi Chirchir on December 14, 2025, before returning to his patrol base in Ndurumo, Rumuruti, and shooting himself.

Another officer attached to Ahero Police Station in Kisumu was found hanging in his house on January 21, 2026. According to an incident report, the officer had previously complained to colleagues about stress linked to unresolved domestic issues.

Beyond the individual tragedies, the incidents raise questions about whether the police service has adequate systems to identify officers experiencing psychological distress, domestic problems or conflicts with colleagues before situations escalate.
They also raise questions about firearm management, particularly when an officer is facing a domestic challenges, disciplinary difficulties or other circumstances that affect mental health.

Gachagua accuses IEBC of state capture ahead of 2027 polls
items.description: DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua declared on Citizen TV's JKLive that no one will steal Kenya's 2027 General Election, accusing the IEBC of operating under state capture.
content: The impeached former Deputy President fires his sharpest warning yet — at the IEBC, President Ruto, and anyone who thinks they can steal the vote

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua returned to prime-time national television on Wednesday night with his most combative performance yet, declaring on Citizen TV’s JKLive that no one would steal the 10 August 2027 General Election on his watch — and accusing the country’s electoral commission of operating under state capture at the direction of President William Ruto.

The interview, broadcast to millions of Kenyans still weighing the country’s fractured political landscape, was not merely a television appearance. It was, in effect, the formal opening salvo of the most consequential election campaign Kenya has seen since 2002. Speaking in his capacity as leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, Gachagua was blunt: no one would be able to rig the election if he was involved, and he would be watching every step of the process.

“I’m an expert in elections; I’ve never lost a presidential election. I have supported presidential candidates even when it looked like it was not fashionable to support Ruto. The day I agreed to support him, he won,” he said, drawing an unmistakable line under his claim to be the opposition’s most formidable electoral strategist.

Kenya’s road to August 2027 is already deeply contested. At its centre stands Gachagua — impeached, unbowed, and operating with the energy of a man who believes history dealt him an injustice he intends to correct at the ballot box. His audience understands the subtext. The Mt Kenya region, which he commands as Kenya’s most populous and historically decisive voting bloc, is watching every move.

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission did not escape the night unscathed. Gachagua accused the IEBC chairman Erastus Ethekon of operating under government influence, alleging the electoral agency was being controlled by the Ministry of Interior. “The chairman is under state capture; IEBC is run by the Ministry of Interior,” he said during the JKLive interview. The IEBC has consistently denied any political interference and has stated publicly that it has nothing to hide.

The interview followed a dramatic day in which Gachagua, alongside United Green Movement leader David Maraga and Democratic Party leader Justin Muturi, boycotted a consultative meeting with the IEBC, claiming it had been organised not by the commission but by the State Department for Interior. “We are not willing to engage in a charade. The meeting this afternoon has been organised by the State Department of Interior. Why is William Ruto speaking for IEBC?” he said at a press briefing earlier in the day.

Gachagua announced that the United Opposition would mobilise Kenyans in January 2027 to engage the commission directly should concerns remain unaddressed. “William Ruto cannot threaten us. Next year in January, we will organise Kenyans to talk to IEBC directly,” he warned.

The accusations are serious — and structurally significant. Kenya’s elections have been disputed before, most catastrophically in 2007 and most controversially in 2017. The spectre of a 2027 contest in which the main opposition does not trust the umpire before a single ballot has been cast raises questions that go far beyond political theatre.

Gachagua has been building this case for weeks. Earlier this month, speaking at the opening of DCP’s Nairobi County offices in Kasarani, he accused the Registrar of Persons of deliberately delaying the issuance of national identity cards to young people in perceived opposition strongholds, claiming applicants in government-aligned areas received their IDs within two to three days while those in opposition areas waited up to seven months. The government dismissed the claims.

On Wednesday night he went further still, alleging that Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo had set aside KSh15 billion to finance political candidates targeting leaders allied to the late Raila Odinga in the 2027 election, with several senior government and parastatal officials expected to resign before 10 February 2027 to seek elective office under the alleged arrangement. Neither Omollo nor the government has responded to the specific allegations.

What gives Gachagua’s warnings their unusual weight is not merely his rhetoric — it is his record and his reach. Since his impeachment, he has constructed a political machine of remarkable speed and discipline. He has sought counsel from Kikuyu elders under the Kiama Kia Kiama leadership, whose guidance, he says, is shaping his strategy towards what he calls the formation of the “sixth administration.” He has opened party offices across the country, fielded candidates successfully in by-elections, and built what observers describe as the most organised opposition structure Kenya has seen heading into a general election.

In October, speaking on KTN, he predicted that the 2027 election would mirror Kenya’s 2002 moment — when opposition parties united behind Mwai Kibaki to end KANU’s decades-long grip on power. He warned that politicians who reject a joint opposition candidate risk political isolation. He has not publicly declared whether he will be that candidate — or whether he will play kingmaker instead — but the ambiguity appears deliberate.

On JKLive, Gachagua addressed the question of his eligibility directly, citing Article 99(3) of the Constitution to argue that he would qualify to be cleared as a presidential candidate. His lawyers have been pursuing the matter through the courts, and observers expect a ruling on his eligibility to become one of the defining legal battles of the pre-election period.

He has also prepared for the possibility of disqualification, revealing that he has identified a pool of young leaders capable of carrying the Mt Kenya region’s presidential bid if courts rule against him, dismissing suggestions that such a ruling would leave the region politically leaderless.

The political arithmetic of 2027 remains fluid. President Ruto retains the advantages of incumbency, state resources, and a party — the United Democratic Alliance — with deep organisational roots. But the economic pain of the past two years, the Gen Z uprising of 2024 that forced a cabinet reshuffle, and the continuing cost-of-living pressures have dented his approval ratings considerably. For many Kenyans, 2027 is not yet decided.

What Wednesday’s interview confirmed is that the campaign is now fully under way — raw, loud, and deeply personal. Gachagua is no longer simply a former official making allegations from the margins. He is the opposition’s most prominent voice, its most effective fundraiser, and arguably its most feared strategist. For a country with Kenya’s electoral history, the combination of a motivated opposition, a disputed umpire, and a sitting president fighting for his political survival makes August 2027 a date every Kenyan is already counting down to.

Whether the vote is clean, credible, and peaceful when it arrives will depend on choices made in the months between now and then. If Wednesday night’s interview is any guide, those months will not be quiet.

items.title: Equity Bank opens door to Kenyans with development proposals
items.description: Equity Bank Kenya has invited individuals and groups to submit socio-economic development proposals via its official email for guidance on available funding and support.
content: The lender says anyone with a clear socio-economic idea can submit it by email — here is exactly how to do it

Equity Bank has explained how Kenyans with ideas for socio-economic development can approach the institution for support, directing interested individuals to submit proposals via the bank’s official email address for assessment and guidance on available opportunities.

In a response issued on Thursday, 19 November 2026, the bank confirmed its commitment to backing initiatives that promote financial inclusion, entrepreneurship, education, agribusiness, and sustainable community development — and said it was open to hearing from anyone with a credible concept.

“Yes, we are committed to supporting socio-economic development through initiatives that promote financial inclusion, entrepreneurship, education, agribusiness, and sustainable community development,” the bank said. “If you have a specific proposal or concept in mind, we encourage you to share it via our official email address, and we will be glad to advise on the available avenues for support.”

The process, as the bank describes it, is straightforward. An applicant should begin with a clear, well-structured proposal — not a general request for money, but a focused document explaining what the idea is, who it will benefit, where it will be implemented, and what measurable change it aims to deliver. That proposal should then be submitted to Equity Bank’s official email address, available on its website, with a brief personal introduction and an explicit request for guidance on what support is available. The bank will respond with advice on next steps, requirements, and the nature of assistance it can offer.

Equity Bank identified five areas its socio-economic development initiatives cover: expanding access to financial services for underserved Kenyans; supporting small businesses and innovators; backing education and leadership development; strengthening agricultural value chains; and funding projects that improve community lives in a lasting and sustainable way.

It is worth noting what the bank did not disclose. No formal application form, specific funding amounts, eligibility criteria, or submission deadlines were published. Whether support will take the form of grants, loans, partnerships, or other arrangements was also left unstated. Prospective applicants will need to seek those details directly from the bank once initial contact is made.

For Kenya’s youth groups, women’s organisations, smallholder farmers, and early-stage entrepreneurs with solid ideas but limited capital, this represents a practical first door. The barrier to entry is low: a clear idea, a coherent write-up, and an email to the right address.
If you have a concept that could genuinely change your community, Equity Bank’s message is simple — write it down, make it compelling, and reach out through the bank’s official channels.

items.title: "Demand is huge": PSC explains how gov't will hire 50k interns in January 2027
items.description: Kenya’s PSC plans 50,000 government internships from January 2027, using a 10% staffing formula as 41,000 graduates compete for 8,000 places amid high demand.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Kenyan graduates could soon have far greater access to government internships after the Public Service Commission outlined plans to grow available placements from 8,000 to 50,000 starting January 2027, following a directive from President William Ruto during the 2026 Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret.

PSC Chairperson Francis Meja explained that the commission had settled on a standardised formula to bring predictability to how positions are spread across ministries, state departments, agencies and parastatals.
Each institution will be required to ring-fence internship slots equal to 10% of its approved staffing establishment, meaning an organisation with 1,000 approved posts would absorb 100 interns.

Previously, the National Treasury channelled roughly KSh 2 billion annually to fund approximately 8,000 internship positions. That figure, however, has long fallen short of demand. When the PSC last advertised 8,000 positions, it received 41,000 applications.
Meja described the internship scheme as a bridge between academic training and the job market, stressing that the target of 50,000 is a starting point rather than a ceiling.

Graduates who complete the programme will reportedly be given priority consideration when institutions post formal vacancies, although completing an internship does not guarantee permanent employment.

The PSC chairperson also revealed that talks with private-sector employers are progressing and that a further 50,000 positions are intended to be unlocked through industry partnerships by January 2027.

The PSC has opened applications for the 2026/2027 financial year, with the deadline set for December 14, 2026. Graduates are urged to apply only through the Commission's official recruitment platforms to avoid falling victim to fraudsters.

Elsewhere, TUKO also highlighted facts about the Public Service Commission’s 6,000 internship positions under the Affordable Housing Programme, including the fields on offer, eligibility requirements and application deadline.

The 12-month placements span technical and professional roles across the country, with 500 construction management slots among the largest allocations. Applications close on November 9, 2026, and candidates must have graduated from 2020 onwards.

items.title: Zamara launches investment business and four unit trust funds
items.description: The new investment business has already accumulated KSh 2.2 billion in Assets Under Management (AUM) since it began receiving investments in May 2026,
content: The launch comes at a time when Kenya’s investment landscape is evolving,

Nairobi, Kenya, 26 November 2026 – Zamara Group today launched Zamara Investments and four Unit Trust Funds, marking a significant milestone in its growth strategy and expansion into Kenya’s investment market.

Following regulatory approval by the Capital Markets Authority (CMA), the Group has introduced four Unit Trust Funds designed to cater to the diverse financial objectives, investment horizons and risk appetites of individuals, businesses and institutional investors.
The four funds comprise the Zamara Money Market Fund (KES), Zamara Money Market Fund (USD), Zamara Fixed Income Fund (KES) and Zamara Global Balanced Special Fund (USD).

The launch builds on the group’s more than three decades of experience in pensions, actuarial services and insurance broking, bringing together three fundamental pillars of financial wellbeing: wealth creation, financial protection and retirement security.

Speaking during the launch, Zamara Group Chief Executive Officer Sundeep Raichura said the expansion into investments represents a natural evolution of the Group’s business and its purpose of creating a financially secure and prosperous society.
Zamara Group Kicks off Discussions on The Road To Universal Health Coverage

“For over three decades, we have helped individuals, families and organisations navigate some of their most important financial decisions. Our entry into investments is a natural evolution of that journey.

“Financial security is not built through pensions or insurance alone. Individuals need opportunities to create wealth, protect what they have accumulated and prepare for the future. Bringing investments into our portfolio of financial solutions, helps us strengthen our ability to support our clients across their entire financial journey and deliver on our promise of Powering Prosperity.

Gideon Chokah, Head of Financing Securities Services (Kenya & East Africa) Standard Chartered Bank, representing Standard Chartered Bank, Trustee and Custodian of the Fund said, “A unit trust does more than bring investors together. It brings together their hopes, ambitions and resources and channels them towards productive opportunities that can improve lives, strengthen businesses and help build the economy.

By pooling savings and directing capital into productive investments, unit trusts contribute to deeper capital markets, support economic activity and help connect the aspirations of individual investors with the growth and development of the wider economy.”

The new investment business has already accumulated KSh 2.2 billion in Assets Under Management (AUM) since it began receiving investments in May 2026, reflecting early investor confidence in Zamara’s investment proposition and providing a strong foundation for its growth ambitions.

The launch comes at a time when Kenya’s investment landscape is evolving, with growing interest in professionally managed investment solutions and increasing demand for accessible and diversified avenues for wealth creation. According to the Capital Markets Authority’s quarterly report, assets held in collective investment schemes reached KSh 948.7 billion at the end of June 2026, an 11 percent rise from KSh 851.7 billion in March. More than four million Kenyans now hold unit trusts, and 98 percent of them are local retail investors.

The market is also maturing, with money market funds which held about 90 percent of industry assets in 2020, today hold roughly half, as investors move into fixed income and special funds in search of higher returns over longer horizons.
The funds will be available through MyZamara, the Group’s digital platform.

Payaza Africa has acquired Seesail Technologies Ltd, a Ghana-founded commerce platform serving small businesses, through its Shopaza product days after the Lagos-based payments company formally entered Kenya.
Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The full Seesail team moves across to Shopaza, and Seesail co-founder and CEO Victor Blavo takes up the role of General Manager, Africa.

The acquisition did not come out of the blue. Seesail's merchants had already been processing payments through Payaza's infrastructure, giving Payaza's leadership an early vantage point on the team's performance before any ownership conversation began.

Payaza CEO Seyi Ebenezer described the deal as a conviction bet on a team that had achieved real traction with limited resources.
Payaza said every Seesail function joins Shopaza with its own budget from day one and the operational freedom to run independently, under guidance from the CEO.
The combined entity is designed to extend Shopaza's commerce infrastructure into access to finance and broader distribution for small and medium-sized enterprises across Africa.

Blavo built Seesail around a conviction shaped by his own family's experience. After his mother attempted to revive a restaurant business she had operated in Yaba, Lagos, following the family's relocation to Ghana, she found that affordable tools and financing were simply unavailable.

That gap became the founding premise of Seesail.
Before bootstrapping Seesail, Blavo accumulated experience across Nigerian, Ghanaian and international firms, including Chipper Cash.

As reported earlier on TUKO.co.ke, Payaza received authorisation from the Central Bank of Kenya on November 17, 2026, to operate as a payment service provider, landing in one of the continent's most active digital payments markets.
Founded in Lagos in 2022, the company now operates across 31 countries spanning Africa, North America, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates and Oceania.
Kenya's payments landscape offers significant scale. Mobile money transactions reached KSh 8.7 trillion in 2024, a figure equivalent to more than half of national GDP.
Payaza's local focus centres on cross-border transfer solutions, merchant acquiring infrastructure and e-commerce tools for merchants and exporters.
The Seesail acquisition broadens the SME toolkit Payaza can deploy across Kenya, Ghana and other markets as it competes with regional players including Paystack, Cellulant and Moniepoint.

content: Kenya Principal Secretary: State Department for ICT and the Digital Economy, John Tanui

from MARIA MACHARIA in Nairobi, Kenya Kenya Bureau NAIROBI, (CAJ News) – THE conclusion of the Kenya-European Union (EU) Digital Dialogue paves the way for increased cooperation in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), data protection, digital public services, online safety and digital trade.
At the conclusion of the dialogue in Brussels, Belgium, the two parties adopted a Joint Communiqué outlining key areas of collaboration.
John Tanui, the Principal Secretary for ICT and the Digital Economy, led the Kenyan delegation to the recently concluded dialogue.
“The aim is to expand trade, attract investment, create jobs in Kenya and open opportunities for EU enterprises,” Tanui said.

On digital infrastructure, the communiqué focuses on advancing investment in 3 000 km of aerial fibre, connectivity for 3 000 schools, health centres and digital hubs, and Wi-Fi for 400 remote communities.
The focus on AI includes deepening collaboration through European AI Factories, €10 million in funding support, AI talent development and plans for an open-access computing facility in Kenya.
The parties welcomed the successful conclusion of technical negotiations on mutual data adequacy to facilitate trusted cross-border data transfers.

The conclusion of the dialogue also paves the way for strengthening business process outsourcing partnerships, business-to-business matchmaking, product traceability and investment in Kenya’s digital and electronics industries, while promoting trusted digital identity, interoperability, open standards and enhanced protection of children online.
The dialogue builds on Kenya’s position as the first African country to establish a formal Digital Dialogue with the EU, in March 2026.
The focus now is to translate these commitments into investments, stronger business partnerships, expanded connectivity and digital employment opportunities for Kenyan youth.

items.title: KAA Seeks Public Views on Proposed 2026 Airport Charges, Sets December Deadline
items.description: Kenya Airports Authority is seeking public views on proposed 2026 commercial charges at airports, with written submissions closing on December 8.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Kenya Airports Authority (KAA) has opened consultations with business organisations and the public over proposed changes to commercial charges at airports across the country.

The authority convened a high-level roundtable in Nairobi on Thursday, November 26, bringing together representatives of ten business member organisations to discuss the proposed Commercial Charges Order, 2026.
KAA Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Moses Wekesa chaired the meeting, which attracted leaders from the cargo, logistics, horticulture, manufacturing and aviation sectors.
The consultations are intended to gather views from businesses that rely on airport services before the proposed charges are finalised.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
The Shippers Council of Eastern Africa and the Kenya International Freight and Warehousing Association (KIFWA) represented the logistics and freight sectors.
Kenya sets deadline for all NGOs to transition to Public Benefits Organisations

The Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya (FPEAK), Kenya Flower Council (KFC) and Fresh Produce Consortium of Kenya represented fresh produce and flower exporters, many of whom transport their goods through Jomo Kenyatta International Airport.
Other participants included the Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM) and Nyamita Miraa Traders.
The aviation sector was represented by the Kenya Association of Air Operators (KAAO), the Airline Operators Committee (AOC) and the International Air Transport Association (IATA).
KAA has invited members of the public and other stakeholders to review the draft Commercial Charges Order, 2026, which is available on the authority's official website.
Written submissions will be accepted until December 8, 2026. The authority has also scheduled regional public barazas for December 9 as part of efforts to extend the consultation beyond Nairobi.

The proposed order outlines commercial fees applicable at KAA-managed airports. Its provisions are particularly relevant to cargo owners, freight forwarders, warehouse operators, airlines and exporters who depend on airport facilities and services.
The authority is seeking feedback from these groups to inform the final document before it comes into effect.

items.title: "It costs KSh 1,000": Huduma Kenya explains adding father's name to birth cert
items.description: Huduma Kenya says adding a father's name to a birth notification costs KSh 1,000 and must be done at a civil registration office in the county of birth in Kenya.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Kenyans who need to add a father's name to a birth notification must travel to the county where the birth was registered, Huduma Kenya has stated, confirming that the amendment cannot be processed from any other location.

The clarification emerged from a public exchange on the official Huduma Kenya Facebook page, after a citizen named Jacqueline asked about the correct procedure for updating a birth notification that had been issued without the father's details.

Huduma Kenya instructed Jacqueline to present herself at Civil Registration offices or a Huduma Centre situated within the county of birth, adding that a registrar would provide further guidance once she arrived.
The response prompted a follow-up from another user who wanted to know whether the county-of-birth requirement was absolute, particularly for people now living in Nairobi.
Huduma Kenya stood by its earlier guidance, confirming that applicants must return to the county where the birth record originated.
The agency also disclosed that the amendment service costs KSh 1,000.

The requirement for county-specific processing reflects how civil registration records are maintained in Kenya, where birth records are held at the district or county level, and amendments must be verified and approved by the registrar responsible for that jurisdiction.

Civil registration matters in Kenya fall under the Births and Deaths Registration Act, which governs how birth records are created, stored, and updated across the country.
Recently, Huduma Kenya clarified whether a father’s name can be removed from a child’s birth certificate .
The agency said the document cannot be changed at a service desk and that Kenyan law permits removal only in limited circumstances.
A parent’s regret or a relationship breakdown is not enough to erase a name from the record.
Even when paternity is disputed, a court must weigh DNA evidence against the child’s right to know their origins and access parental support.

items.title: CAF AFCON PAMOJA 2027 secretariat opened in Dar es Salaam
items.description: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) opened the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) PAMOJA 2027 Secretariat Headquarters in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania on Wednesday.
content: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) opened the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) PAMOJA 2027 Secretariat Headquarters in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania on Wednesday.

The inauguration marked a significant milestone in the collective preparations by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda to jointly host Africa’s premier football tournament, reinforcing regional cooperation, institutional coordination and collective accountability.

The inauguration was followed by a PAMOJA Oversight Committee meeting chaired by CAF General Secretary Samson Adamu, during which the overall preparedness, infrastructure development and operational readiness of the three countries were assessed.
The initiative is central to the three countries’ ambition of delivering AFCON as one integrated hosting partnership.

The meeting further reviewed progress towards the operationalisation of the PAMOJA Visa, bringing together relevant immigration and government authorities to facilitate seamless cross-border movement of teams, officials, supporters and tournament equipment.

CAF lauded Kenya’s progress in the ongoing works at the Raila Odinga International Stadium at Talanta Sports City, Kasarani Stadium and the 12 designated training pitches across Nairobi, which remain on schedule towards attaining full compliance with CAF standards.
CAF also presented the PAMOJA tournament identity, whose shield symbolism reflects the shared heritage, sovereignty and collective identity of the three host nations.
Deliberations focused on leveraging national tourism boards and relevant government institutions to drive joint promotional campaigns, destination marketing and fan engagement.

Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda remain united in their commitment to delivering a world-class AFCON that strengthens regional integration, showcases East Africa’s sporting excellence and cultural diversity, and positions the region as a premier global sporting, tourism and investment destination.

80 JKUAT students showcase solutions from Samsung Innovation Campus
items.description: Eighty JKUAT students in 17 teams presented digital solutions at the Samsung Innovation Campus showcase - Read more.
content: Students taking part in the Samsung Innovation Campus (SIC) programme have presented digital solutions to local problems at a showcase at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT).
The event, held at JKUAT’s main campus in Juja, was hosted by the university’s technology incubation centre, JHUB Africa, with Samsung Electronics East Africa.

Samsung Innovation Campus is Samsung’s global education programme, which trains young people in industry-relevant digital skills, including artificial intelligence (AI), coding and programming. In Kenya, it runs through a partnership between Samsung Electronics East Africa, JKUAT and JHUB Africa. Samsung said JKUAT is the only university in East Africa running the programme.
This cohort had 80 students working in 17 teams. Each team had to identify a local problem and build a technology solution to address it.
The “Smart Nyuki” team took first place with a solution that helps local beekeepers manage their hives.
“One of the most valuable aspects of this programme has been the opportunity to move beyond learning concepts and actually build something,” said Moses Njau, a member of the winning team.
“Working on our projects has helped us understand how technology can be applied to solve problems, while also strengthening our technical and problem-solving skills.”

Nyawira Muraguri, Head of Corporate Marketing at Samsung Electronics East Africa, said equipping young people with digital skills is central to the company’s commitment to creating opportunities through technology.
“Through the Samsung Innovation Campus, we are investing in young people by equipping them with the skills and confidence to become creators of technology, not just consumers of it,” said Muraguri.
“The projects being presented today demonstrate what is possible when young talent is given access to the right knowledge, tools and opportunities to innovate.”

Beyond classroom learning, the programme gives participants practical exposure to technology and helps them build problem-solving, critical thinking and innovation skills. Samsung said it links academic knowledge with industry needs

Kenya and Pakistan Move to Deepen Health Cooperation
items.description: Kenya and Pakistan Move to Deepen Health Cooperation Kenya News Agency
content: The Cabinet Secretary (CS) for Health, Aden Duale held bilateral talks with Pakistan’s Federal Minister for National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, Syed Mustafa Kamal, in Karachi, as the two countries work to formalize a structured Government-to-Government partnership in the health sector.
The meeting, hosted at Aga Khan University, marks a significant step towards concluding a Health Memorandum of Understanding that has been under negotiation since 2021.

The central focus of the discussions was the existing pharmaceutical trade relationship between the two nations. Pakistan currently exports 247 registered medicines to Kenya, with annual imports valued at approximately Sh1.4 billion.
In addition, 26 Pakistani manufacturing facilities have received Good Manufacturing Practice certification from Kenya’s Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB).

Duale emphasised the importance of moving beyond informal trade relations to a formalized framework with clear priorities and accountability mechanisms, enabling both countries to maximize the benefits of cooperation.
At the meeting, Kenya proposed a cooperation framework built on three pillars: regulatory cooperation, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and specialist training.

Under regulatory cooperation, the partnership aims to strengthen collaboration between the PPB and Pakistan’s Drug Regulatory Authority through information sharing and joint inspections, with the goal of improving access to safe, quality-assured medicines in both markets.
On manufacturing, the Cabinet Secretary encouraged Pakistani pharmaceutical companies to invest in Kenya’s industrial parks and Special Economic Zones.

“Such investments would support local production, technology transfer and industrial growth, while positioning Kenya as a regional pharmaceutical manufacturing and export hub serving the East African Community and the wider African Continental Free Trade Area,” he noted.

To tackle shortages in specialist healthcare personnel, particularly in oncology and nephrology, Kenya proposed an annual placement programme for Kenyan medical fellows in Pakistan’s specialised training institutions, with the first cohort targeted for 2027.

Similarly, the talks also explored cooperation in digital health, specifically drawing on Pakistan’s experience to strengthen Kenya’s pharmaceutical track-and-trace systems, in line with each country’s data protection and regulatory frameworks.

The meeting was hosted by Aga Khan University Vice-Chancellor and President Dr Sulaiman Shahabuddin and attended by Kenya’s High Commissioner to Pakistan, Lt Gen (Rtd) Peter Njiru, and Pharmacy and Poisons Board Chief Executive Officer Dr Ahmed Mohammed.

With the proposed framework, both countries appear positioned to convert years of trade engagement into a formal, mutually beneficial health partnership. The conclusion of the long-pending Memorandum of Understanding would provide the institutional foundation needed to drive regulatory alignment, investment and workforce development – outcomes with tangible implications for medicine access and healthcare capacity in Kenya and the wider region.

Murang’a determined to reduce child stunting to below five percent
items.description: Murang’a determined to reduce child stunting to below five percent Kenya News Agency
content: Murang’a County has set an ambitious target of reducing childhood stunting to below five per cent by 2030 as it rolls out a five-year nutrition action plan aimed at tackling all forms of malnutrition and improving household feeding practices.

The Second County Nutrition Action Plan (CNAP II), covering the period 2026–2031 seeks to address stunting, wasting, underweight, overweight, obesity and micronutrient deficiencies through coordinated interventions involving health, agriculture, education, water, trade, gender and social services.

Speaking during the launch at the County Headquarters on Wednesday, Deputy Governor Stephen Munania stated that the strategy would strengthen preventive healthcare while integrating nutrition into the county’s agricultural and education programmes.
He singled out the expanded school feeding programme which will commence in January 2027 and cover public primary schools, Junior Schools and Early Childhood Development (ECD) centres.
The programme, he noted, will provide meals at Sh15 per plate, with the county targeting more than 250,000 plates daily to improve learners’ nutrition, school attendance and concentration.
Munania added that the initiative would also create a reliable market for local farmers by sourcing food supplies, including vegetables, mangoes and milk, within the county.
He noted that linking school feeding to local agricultural production would improve farmers’ incomes while ensuring learners access nutritious meals.
“We want to create an economy around food, an economy around nutrition and an economy around education while ensuring our farmers benefit more,” he remarked.

The County Nutrition Coordinator Nancy Mwangi explained the new plan builds on the first County Nutrition Action Plan, implemented between 2020 and 2025, which contributed to reducing childhood stunting from 19.2 per cent in 2014 to 10 per cent.

She said the county was targeting to reduce the rate to below five per cent by 2030 through improved maternal and child nutrition, nutrition education and increased access to diverse and balanced diets.
However, she noted that nutritional challenges persisted among different population groups, with 43 per cent of adolescent boys being too thin for their age, compared to 12 percent of girls.
She added that 27 per cent of women were overweight or obese, while 17 per cent of men were underweight. Among children, six per cent were underweight, while ten per cent were experiencing stunting.

Mwangi urged households to improve their feeding habits by ensuring daily meals comprised at least five of the ten recognized food groups, noting that dietary diversity was essential in preventing malnutrition and related illnesses.
“Food is medicine. If we don’t take food as medicine, we will take medicine as food,” she stated.

The nutritionist added that the county would intensify nutrition education at the grassroots to equip families with knowledge on locally available nutritious foods, food preparation and balanced diets.

Meanwhile, Nutrition International representative Dr Elijah Mbiti observed that inadequate nutrition knowledge and poor household food choices continued to undermine efforts to address malnutrition, even in communities with sufficient food production.
Mbiti noted that some households prioritized selling nutritious farm produce without setting aside enough for their children’s dietary needs.

“Some households produce eggs but sell all of them, yet the children in those homes also need these eggs for their nutritional needs,” he said, urging families to balance income generation with household nutritional requirements.

The five-year plan brings together county departments, development partners and communities in a coordinated effort to improve nutrition outcomes through better access to nutritious foods, strengthened healthcare services and increased public awareness.

The strategy places emphasis on prevention, recognizing that tackling malnutrition requires more than adequate food production and must also involve better feeding practices, household awareness and access to essential nutrition services.
